extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal advisers, and law students studying patentability doctrines
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the qualities of invention required for a valid patent (novelty, proper claiming, and when applying known things to new uses is or is not patentable). Focuses on how to draft and construe claims so the true invention — method, property, or combination — is captured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double use / analogous use objection
rubrics_metrics.description: "that in order to escape the objection of a double use, it is necessary that the new occasion or purpose to which the use of a known thing is applied should not be merely analogous to the former occasions or purposes to which the same thing has been applied."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a known contrivance or method is applied to a new purpose but produces no new mode of operation or new effect, the application is a "double use" and not patentable. Illustrations: using a caisson under water when it had been used on land; fixing spinning-machine rollers at a particular distance when the machine could already be adjusted; applying an old machine to an analogous substance (cotton/linen to wool) without substantive change. Anti-patterns: claiming as new merely the transfer of a known device to an analogous purpose or material.

rubrics_metrics.name: New application must produce a new effect or development of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The new occasion or purpose must not be merely analogous — it should produce some new effect or exhibit a "new development of properties of matter" which was not heretofore known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications of old devices to new ends can be patentable when they lead to a novel mode of operation or reveal/use a previously unknown property (contrast purely analogous applications which are unpatentable). Example: the lead-pipe case where the discovery that set lead reunites under heat and pressure produced a new practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a new property of matter can support patentability when practically applied
rubrics_metrics.description: When a newly discovered property of matter is made practically useful by applying a (possibly old) combination of machinery, the combination as applied may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: discovery that lead, when recently set and still hot, will reunite perfectly under extreme pressure; substituting a short immovable core and bridge to exploit that property produced a new, patentable process/article even if parts of the machinery were old. Caveat: the claim must not be drafted so that novelty of the machinery becomes essential to the patentee's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must describe the real invention; avoid claiming unrelated structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who claims the structure of the machine itself (when the real invention is a new application or method) may hazard the patentable quality of his invention upon the novelty of that machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the caisson case — the plaintiff claimed "the mode of constructing the interior of a caisson..." but by describing the caisson structure prominently, the patent turned on novelty of the caisson apparatus rather than the method of building foundations under water. Drafting guidance: claim the proper improvement (the method or developed use), and avoid unnecessarily making known apparatus the critical novel element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and skill in claim drafting affects scope and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of a claim can limit or change what the patentee is effectively claiming (e.g., claiming a combination "when used" in a particular manner may be construed to require novelty in the machinery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly phrased claims can be construed to make the novelty of old components essential; courts will read claims and may refuse the broader construction the patentee intended. Draft claims to manifest the patentee's true purpose and to avoid unintended limitations (use clear linkage of elements to the novel function or property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely substituting analogous materials or well-known contrivances is not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of one well-known and analogous material for another, or taking a well-known mechanical contrivance and applying it to an analogous purpose, does not of itself constitute a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying wooden planking to an iron frame (Jordan v. Moore) or taking a button/button-hole contrivance into another analogous mechanical combination. Practitioners should identify any substantive mechanical difference or new effect produced by the substitution; if none exists, the claim likely fails for want of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will compare specifications and constructions to determine novelty and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts compare the respective specifications of competing patents (or prior uses) to declare what each covered and whether the claimed matter was new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges may direct verdicts based on comparison of specifications; evidence of prior use of substantially the same combination may be fatal. Practitioners should draft specifications to clearly show the matter the patentee regards as novel and how it differs from prior art; be aware courts will parse claim language in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of novelty required — minor configurational differences may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere slight difference in configuration or shape of an article may not suffice for novelty if the mechanical effect and application are essentially the same as prior devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harwood (fish-plate) illustrates that a groove versus flange-based channel that accomplishes substantially the same function may be held not novel. Emphasize functional/structural distinctions that materially affect performance; trivial or insubstantial differences are unlikely to support a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: An old combination used for a genuinely new method can be patentable if properly claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of an invention may consist in the application of an old combination of machinery to a new end as part of a new process, provided the claim does not make novelty of the machinery essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using an otherwise old machine combination as one element in a new process (e.g., spinning combined with prior maceration). Draft claims to capture the process or the novel application rather than gratuitously claiming old machinery elements standing alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of overbroad claims that hinge on novelty of known parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims which 'hazard the entire patentable quality' on a single issue of novelty of a known component (e.g., the caisson) risk invalidation if that component is shown to be old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming too broadly (or for the whole apparatus) when the patentee's true inventive contribution is a specific application, method, or property exploitation. Narrow, focused claims on the improvement reduce the risk that prior art in unrelated parts will invalidate the whole patent.
